title: Viradha
hook: the giant falls, and at the edge of a freshly dug pit he suddenly remembers who he used to be

segments.voice: Yesterday: Viradha, part one. The giant seized Sita, mocked the brothers, and carried them off until they broke his arms. Did you stay close to someone in a hard moment? Day five hundred fifty-four.

Here's the problem. Viradha is down, arms broken, but he can't be killed with weapons. Brahma's boon still holds. So what do you do with an enemy who can't die the ordinary way? Rama looks at the ground. He tells Lakshmana to dig a pit, a deep one, big enough for a body that size. And while Lakshmana digs, Rama puts his foot on Viradha's throat to hold him down. That's when the giant's face changes.
screen: `AN ENEMY WHO CAN'T DIE.` → `DIG A PIT.` → `THE GIANT'S FACE CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Viradha looks up and recognizes him. You're Rama, he says. Kausalya's son. I was told you would come. And then he tells his story. He wasn't always a forest giant. He was a gandharva, one of the celestial musicians, named Tumburu. He served Kubera, the lord of wealth. But he fell in love with Rambha, one of the apsaras, and in his longing he neglected his duty and didn't show up when he was supposed to. Kubera cursed him: become a rakshasa, a terror of the forest. Tumburu begged for mercy, and Kubera set a limit. When Rama, son of Dasharatha, kills you in battle, you'll be released and return to heaven. So the thing Viradha has been waiting for, all those years of being monstrous, was this. He even tells them how to finish it. Bury me, he says, it's the way for one like me. And one more thing. A few miles from here lives a great sage, Sharabhanga. Go to him. He'll help you. So the brothers lower him into the pit, and as the earth covers him, Viradha leaves the body and rises, released. Notice the turn. Yesterday, he was the forest's first monster. Today he's a cursed musician who has been waiting for someone to set him free. The Ramayana does this again and again: under a terrifying face, a story, a curse, and a release. The enemy becomes the guide who points the way.
screen: `YOU'RE RAMA. I WAS TOLD YOU'D COME.` · `TUMBURU, A CURSED MUSICIAN.` · `BURY ME. GO TO SHARABHANGA.` · `RISING, RELEASED.` · then, large: `THE ENEMY BECOMES THE GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who frightened or frustrated you this year, at work, online, in the family. Hold them lightly, at a distance. Now imagine there's a story under their behavior you don't know: a loss, a pressure, an old hurt. You don't need to invent it, and you don't need to excuse anything. Just let the possibility be there. Breathe in, and let the picture soften a little. The bell holds the time.
Viradha. A gandharva named Tumburu, cursed to be a giant until Rama came. Buried, he rises free, and sends Rama to Sharabhanga.
Your line: the enemy becomes the guide. Today, when someone seems monstrous, remember there may be a story underneath you can't see. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu storytellers often point to Viradha as the first of several beings in the Ramayana released from a curse by meeting Rama, a pattern many devotees read as a sign of his grace.

fork.setup: you're Rama. the giant is down but can't be killed by any weapon. what do you do?
options: leave him there with broken arms.
bury him in a deep pit.
ask the sages to curse him.
fork.reveal: Lakshmana digs a pit. Viradha, recognizing Rama, tells his story and asks to be buried, and rises released.

original.note: Sanskrit gandharva: a celestial musician. Viradha was one, named Tumburu, before Kubera's curse.

trapdoor: what you thought: Viradha is a monster Rama defeats.
what it means: he's a cursed gandharva, freed by meeting Rama.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 4 gives the curse and its limit; this pattern of curse and release recurs with other beings Rama meets.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 4 (Viradha's story; the burial; Sharabhanga)

notes: Tumburu, Kubera and Rambha as given in Aranya 4 (vulgate): confirm names and the cause of the curse.
Viradha's line that burial is the way for one like him: paraphrased; confirm.
'Rama's foot on his throat' while Lakshmana digs: confirm detail.
Devotional reading of curse-and-release as Rama's grace is attributed to devotees, not stated as the text's claim.
